question_text: A previously healthy 16-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a pruritic rash on the chest that has become progressively larger over the past 10 days. It is not painful. He is sexually active with two female partners and uses condoms inconsistently. He works part-time as a lifeguard. He has no family history of serious illness. He does not smoke. He drinks 5–6 beers on weekends. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 66/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. A photograph of the rash is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

                    ### Question

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with a pruritic rash on the chest that has progressively enlarged over 10 days. The lack of pain and the chronic nature of the rash suggest a non-infectious etiology, such as contact dermatitis or an inflammatory skin condition rather than an acute infection or sexually transmitted disease (STD). Given the patient's occupation as a lifeguard, exposure to irritants or allergens is plausible. Topical hydrocortisone is effective for managing inflammatory skin conditions and would address the itching and inflammation associated with contact dermatitis. While topical miconazole could be considered for a fungal infection, the characteristics of the rash and the absence of pain make hydrocortisone a more appropriate first-line treatment. Reassurance may also be appropriate if the condition is self-limiting, but proactive management with hydrocortisone is favored. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is topical hydrocortisone.
